title: Kids Are Pickier About AI Than Adults Assume
hook: MIT Technology Review asked kids aged 10 to 18 what they think of AI. Not cheating, not wonder — mostly a shrug, some hard boundaries, and worry about their own thinking.
key_points: MIT Technology Review interviewed kids aged 10–18 and expected cheating stories; it found nuance instead.
Many use AI for homework help, grammar, or code — while keeping writing, drawing, and music for themselves.
Pew data cited: 57% of US teens used chatbots to look things up, 54% for schoolwork, 47% for fun, just 12% for emotional support.
One 17-year-old, Winter, fears AI will be 'the end of creativity and critical thinking'.
Another teen avoids AI entirely over data-center water use and heat.
content_html: MIT Technology Review talked to kids aged 10 to 18 about artificial intelligence and expected the familiar story: quiet cheating on one side, wide-eyed enthusiasm on the other. What the reporters got back was more careful than that. Plenty of kids find AI unremarkable, and several described firm limits on where they'll let it near their work.
extra_html:
The pattern is selective, not sweeping. Kids reach for AI on tasks they treat as chores — checking grammar, getting unstuck on homework, debugging code — and keep the things they take pride in, like writing, drawing, and music, for themselves. Pew Research figures from February 2026, cited in the piece, back that up: 57% of US teens had used chatbots to look something up and 54% for schoolwork, but only 12% for emotional support.

Their worries also sound less like adult worries. Winter, 17, told the reporters she is "afraid it's going to be the end of creativity and critical thinking." Hazel avoids AI altogether over what data centers do to water and local ecosystems. Read as a whole, the interviews describe young people negotiating with a technology rather than being swept along by it. The full piece, with six profiles, is at MIT Technology Review.

related.title: AI, Kids & School
related.hook: Banning AI is like banning calculators — futile and beside the point. The real job is teaching kids to use it honestly, to learn with it, and to know when it's lying.

related.title: AI as a Tutor
related.hook: A chatbot is a tutor with infinite patience: ask it to explain anything five different ways at any level, with no judgment. Just remember it can be confidently wrong.

related.title: Over-Relying on AI
related.hook: The subtle risk isn't that AI fails — it's that it usually works, so you stop checking. Trusting a confident machine over your own judgment is its own kind of mistake.

related.title: Half of Americans Use Chatbots — Most Think AI Is Moving Too Fast
related.hook: A new Pew poll captures the mood of the AI era: chatbot use has jumped to about half of Americans, yet nearly two-thirds say the technology is advancing too quickly.

flashcards.prompt: What surprised the reporters most about how kids talk about AI?

choices.text: Many were unimpressed or had real reservations, rather than eager to cheat
Nearly all of them had never heard of chatbots
They used AI mainly as an emotional confidant

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors went in expecting cheating stories and inspiring use cases, and instead found "tons of nuance" — including kids who found AI dull or objected to it outright.

flashcards.prompt: Where do the kids interviewed tend to draw the line on using AI?
flashcards.back_html: They accept it for chores like homework help, grammar checks, and coding, but protect creative work — writing, drawing, music — as theirs to do.

flashcards.prompt: Per the Pew figures cited, what did the fewest US teens use chatbots for?
flashcards.explanation_html: Information search (57%), schoolwork (54%), and entertainment (47%) all dwarf emotional support (12%), despite headlines about AI companions.
